name: Ray Charles
hook: A blind pianist who put a gospel song's shape under a secular love song in 1954, one of the records later counted among the first soul music, and who later won ownership of his own master tapes.

blurb.age13: Ray Charles was born in Albany, Georgia, in 1930 and grew up in Greenville, Florida. He was blind by the age of seven. In 1952 he signed to Atlantic Records in New York. In 1954 he heard a gospel song on the radio while on tour and used its shape for 'I Got a Woman', a song about a girlfriend instead of God. Some church people were upset, but mixing church music with love songs became the basis of soul music. In 1959 'What'd I Say' was his first big pop hit. When he moved to the ABC-Paramount label he got a deal in which he would own his master recordings, which almost no Black musician had at the time. He died in 2004.
blurb.adult: Born in Albany, Georgia, on 23 September 1930, raised in Greenville, Florida, and blind by seven, likely from glaucoma. Ahmet Ertegun signed him to Atlantic in 1952. 'I Got a Woman', recorded on 18 November 1954 at the Atlanta studio of the radio station WGST, built a secular love song on the Southern Tones' gospel record 'It Must Be Jesus', which he had heard on the radio that summer; he at first claimed sole authorship. Wikipedia's article on the song calls it one of the prototypes for what was later termed soul music, and 'What'd I Say' (1959), mixing gospel, jazz, blues and Latin rhythm, was his first pop top ten. His move to ABC-Paramount around 1959 to 1960 included eventual ownership of his master tapes, an unusual deal for any artist then and more so for a Black one. 'Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music' (1962) took country songs into the R&B and pop mainstream. He died in Beverly Hills on 10 June 2004.
